units.title: Commas and Periods
units.recap: Commas separate items in a series, join two independent clauses with a connector, follow introductory clauses, and fence off nonessential matter — always in pairs. Two independent clauses joined by a bare comma is a comma splice. Set off direct address, city-and-state, and the year in a full date — and remember the comma after the state and after the year.

errors.explanation: Without the serial comma, “the trustee and the hospital” can read as a renaming of “her children.” In a dispositive document, that ambiguity is expensive.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by a bare comma is a comma splice. Use a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a connector.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by “and” take a comma at the end of the first clause. (Very short clauses — “I paint and he writes” — may skip it.)

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Test: could you say “tedious, long hearing” or “long and tedious hearing”? Both work, so the adjectives are coordinate and take a comma.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A sentence that opens with a dependent clause takes a comma before the main clause. Without it the reader garden-paths into “enforceable the claim.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Nonessential matter midsentence must be enclosed by commas on both sides. The closing one — the Blue Book calls it the appositive comma — is the one writers forget.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: City and state take a comma between them — and another after the state when the sentence continues.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: In a full month-day-year date, the year is fenced by commas on both sides. The Blue Book flags the missing second comma as the one “most people forget.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A name in direct address is enclosed by commas: “Will you, Ms. Okafor, address …” One comma of the pair is missing.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A quotation that comes before the attribution ends with a comma — inside the quotation marks.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: “Therefore,” “however,” and their kin cannot splice two independent clauses with commas. Use a semicolon before the connector and a comma after it.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: “Etc.” takes a comma before it and, midsentence, a comma after it as well.

units.title: Semicolons and Colons
units.recap: A semicolon links two closely related independent clauses, precedes however/therefore/namely when they introduce a full sentence, and separates series items that already contain commas. A colon means “here's what I mean”: it introduces a series or an explanation, and must follow a complete clause — never a bare verb or preposition. Don't use a semicolon where a colon belongs.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A semicolon separates; a colon announces. What follows explains the goal, so the colon is right.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Don't put a colon between a verb and its objects. Either drop it or complete the clause first: “The elements are four: duty, …”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: When the series items already contain commas, promote the separators to semicolons — otherwise the reader can't tell where one city ends and the next begins.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side. “Although the parties settled” is dependent, so a comma is correct.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Use a semicolon before however/therefore/namely when what follows is a complete sentence, and keep the comma after it.

items.prompt: Which capitalization follows the Blue Book?
options: The reason is simple: the statute says so. (lowercase — closely related clause)
The reason is simple: The statute says so. (always capitalize)
Either is defensible; authorities are divided on capitalizing a full sentence after a colon.
items.explanation: The Blue Book is candid here: when a complete sentence follows a colon, authorities are divided. Some always capitalize; some capitalize only formal or general statements. Pick a policy and hold it — this app's house style capitalizes.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: No colon after “such as,” “including,” or any preposition that would need no punctuation on its own.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Once semicolons separate the series, they carry through the final junction: “; and two former auditors.” Half-converted lists are a common draft artifact.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Do not capitalize an ordinary word after a semicolon — the sentence has not ended.

items.prompt: Which is correct in a formal letter to a judge?
items.explanation: A colon follows the salutation in formal correspondence — a comma only in informal notes, and a semicolon never.

units.title: Question Marks and Quotation Marks
units.recap: Periods and commas always go inside closing quotation marks in American style. Question marks and exclamation points follow logic — inside if the quoted matter is the question, outside if the whole sentence is. Use single quotes only for a quotation inside a quotation. Indirect questions take a period, not a question mark.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Periods and commas always go inside the closing quotation mark in American usage — regardless of logic.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Semicolons and colons go outside the closing quotation mark — the exact opposite of periods and commas.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The quoted maxim is not a question; the sentence is. So the question mark sits outside the quotation marks. Question marks follow sense.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: This is an indirect question — a statement that reports a question — so it takes a period. Only direct questions take question marks.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Which correctly nests a quotation inside a quotation?
options: She testified, “He said, ‘I never signed it.’ ”
She testified, “He said, “I never signed it.” ”
She testified, ‘He said, “I never signed it.” ’
items.explanation: American style: double quotes outside, single inside. Note the courtesy space between the adjacent single and double marks — and the period tucked inside both.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Single quotation marks are valid only inside another quotation. Scare quotes and terms used in an unusual way take double marks.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: When a quoted question ends midsentence, the question mark replaces the comma — you never need both.

items.prompt: Which is punctuated as the Blue Book recommends?
options: Why don't you take a break.
Why don't you take a break?
Why don't you take a break!?
items.explanation: Rhetorical questions — statements or requests wearing a question's clothes — are often better with a period. They don't expect an answer.

items.prompt: Which sentence quotes correctly?
options: He said that he “hoped the panel would rule quickly.”
He said, “I hope the panel rules quickly.”
items.explanation: Quotation marks mean word-for-word. The first sentence paraphrases (“he said that he hoped”) and then dresses the paraphrase up as a quotation — which misrepresents the speaker.

units.title: Parentheses and Brackets
units.recap: Parentheses hold asides and clarifications. If the whole sentence is inside them, the period goes inside; if only a fragment, the period goes outside. Parentheses are not part of the subject. Commas follow parentheses, never precede them. Brackets are used only inside quoted material — to explain, to alter, or to flag a source's own error with [sic].

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The parenthetical is a fragment, not a sentence, so the period belongs outside the closing parenthesis — and the sentence still needs one.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Commas follow parentheses rather than preceding them: “When the mandate issued (the clerk had already left), the case was closed.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Parentheses are not part of the subject. The subject is trustee, singular — was present. (If that reads oddly, rewrite the sentence.)

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: [Sic] goes in brackets, not parentheses — brackets signal that someone other than the original author inserted the material. Italicize sic itself.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
You must capitalize a quoted word that was lowercase in the source. Write:
items.explanation: Brackets preserve the integrity of both the quotation and your sentence. Silent alteration misquotes; parentheses don't signal alteration.

items.prompt: Which is correct?
items.explanation: The question mark belongs to the parenthetical; the period closes the whole sentence. Both marks are doing separate jobs.

items.prompt: When are brackets appropriate?
items.explanation: The Blue Book is firm: parentheses and brackets are never interchangeable, and brackets are used exclusively inside quotations.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A fragment inside parentheses takes its period outside: “… (except the chief judge).”

units.title: Apostrophes
units.recap: Singular possession adds ’s. Regular plurals take the apostrophe after the s; irregular plurals (children, teeth) form the plural first, then add ’s. Never use an apostrophe to make a name or noun plural. Joint possession marks only the last owner; separate possession marks both. Possessive pronouns — its, yours, hers, theirs, whose — never take apostrophes. Watch for false possessives.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Children is already plural — there is no such word as “childrens.” Form the plural first, then add ’s: children's.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A family named Jones is “the Joneses”; their home is the Joneses'. “The Jones'” would belong to a family named Jone.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Never use an apostrophe to make a name plural. More than one Wilson = the Wilsons.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Separate possession marks both owners: Reyes's and Nakamura's separate declarations. Joint possession would mark only the last.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The apostrophe goes exactly where the letters were removed — doesn't (do + es + n[o]t).

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A plain plural takes no apostrophe. The greengrocer's apostrophe is the most visible error on this list.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Amounts of time and money act as possessives: three weeks' leave, a week's notice, my two cents' worth.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A false possessive: “United States” is doing adjective work here, and adjectives rarely take apostrophes. Same with “a Beatles song.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Plural of a noun ending in y is -ies; the plural possessive is -ies'. Three companies' policies.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Possessive pronouns never take apostrophes: hers, ours, yours, theirs, its, whose.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: The mark before a shortened year is an apostrophe (’), which curls like a comma — not an opening single quotation mark (‘). Word processors get this wrong constantly.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

units.title: Hyphens Between Words
units.recap: Hyphenate two or more words acting as a single modifier before a noun; after the noun, usually leave them open. Use suspended hyphens in paired modifiers (three- to four-week). Never hyphenate “very” or an -ly adverb to what it modifies. Ages take hyphens unless the time period is plural. Add a hyphen whenever it prevents a misreading.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Two words acting as one modifier before a noun take a hyphen: a good-faith exception. After the noun it opens up: the exception applies in good faith.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: After the noun the compound normally opens: an off-campus apartment, but the apartment is off campus. (A few set phrases — state-of-the-art — keep their hyphens everywhere.)

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Never hyphenate an -ly adverb to the word it modifies. The -ly already does the linking.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Suspended hyphen: “a three- to four-week delay,” which is shorthand for “a three-week to four-week delay.”

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Ages before a noun need BOTH hyphens. With only one, the sentence describes an “old child” who is two years.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Which hyphen prevents a real misreading?
options: Neither — the phrase is never ambiguous.
items.explanation: Without the hyphen, was the permit hidden, or was it a permit for concealed weapons? The hyphen binds concealed+weapons into one modifier and settles it.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Hyphenate all compound numbers from twenty-one through ninety-nine.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Hyphenate spelled-out fractions: two-thirds. (But “a third” and “a half” stay open.)

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Do not hyphenate a multi-word proper noun used as a compound adjective.

items.prompt: The Blue Book says which about “a high school senior” vs. “a high-school senior”?
options: Both are defensible — familiar set phrases may go unhyphenated, but hyphenating all compound modifiers is also accepted
Only the hyphenated form is correct
Only the open form is correct
items.explanation: Editors split on well-known expressions (high school, ice cream, twentieth century). Pick a policy, be consistent, and look up anything you're unsure of.

units.title: Hyphens with Prefixes and Suffixes
units.recap: Hyphenate a prefix before a proper noun (mid-July, trans-American). Always hyphenate self-, ex- (meaning former), and all-. Use a hyphen after re- when omitting it would create a different word (re-cover vs. recover). Great- takes a hyphen in family names; grand- does not. Suffixes are usually closed up, with a few exceptions like -elect, -free, and -style.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Hyphenate a prefix that lands on a proper noun or proper adjective: mid-July, trans-American, post-Erie.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Always hyphenate self-, ex- (former), and all-: ex-mayor, self-executing, all-knowing.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Self- always takes a hyphen — even in predicate position, unlike ordinary compound modifiers.

items.prompt: Which sentence means the sofa was upholstered a second time?
options: I have re-covered the sofa twice.
I have recovered the sofa twice.
items.explanation: The hyphen after re- prevents collision with a different word: re-cover (cover again) vs. recover (get back or get well). Same with re-press vs. repress.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.
Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Great- takes a hyphen in family names; grand- closes up (grandson, granduncle). Half brother and half sister stay open.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Suffixes are usually closed, but -elect, -free, -based, and -style are hyphenated: mayor-elect, sugar-free, oil-based.

items.prompt: Why do many writers hyphenate “co-worker”?
options: Without the hyphen, “coworker” starts with “cow” and distracts the reader
items.explanation: The Blue Book's own reasoning: hyphenate a prefix when the closed form would be distracting or confusing (de-ice, co-worker).

items.prompt: Which does the Blue Book recommend?
items.explanation: Prefixes ending in a vowel are often hyphenated before the same vowel (ultra-ambitious, semi-invalid), but pre- and re- before e are an explicit exception — close them up.

items.prompt: Which is correct?
items.explanation: Prefix + proper adjective → hyphen.

units.title: Dashes, Ellipses, Exclamation Points, and Slashes
units.recap: Em dashes mark an interruption or abrupt turn and replace whatever punctuation would otherwise be there — in pairs, when midsentence. Words between dashes are not part of the subject. En dashes handle number ranges and open compounds (New York–based). Ellipses show omitted words from a quotation. Exclamation points have no place in formal writing, and the slash rarely earns its keep.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: A dash opened midsentence must be closed by a dash. Mixed dash–comma pairs are among the easiest errors to read straight past.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: Like parentheses, words between dashes are not part of the subject. The subject is trustee, singular: the trustee—and her accountant—was present.

items.prompt: Which uses an en dash correctly?
options: During the years 1999–2016, the firm doubled in size.
During the years 1999—2016, the firm doubled in size.
During the years 1999-to-2016, the firm doubled in size.
items.explanation: En dashes (shorter than em dashes, longer than hyphens) carry number ranges: 1999–2016, 3:15–3:45 p.m., 300–325 people.

items.prompt: Which punctuates the open compound as the Blue Book suggests?
items.explanation: For open compounds like New York or Charles Dickens, an en dash makes the modifier read clearly — though a hyphen is also accepted.

items.prompt: The full quotation is “Today, after hours of careful thought, the governor vetoed the bill.” Which is a proper trim?
items.explanation: An ellipsis marks omitted words. Silently deleting them — option two — misrepresents the source, and parentheses don't signal omission.

items.prompt: In formal business or legal writing, exclamation points are:
items.explanation: The Blue Book quotes Fitzgerald: “An exclamation point is like laughing at your own joke.” Avoid them in formal writing.

items.prompt: Correct the error — or submit with nothing flagged if the sentence is already right.

errors.explanation: An exclamation point replaces a midsentence comma as well as a period — you never use both.

items.prompt: Which does the Blue Book prefer in formal writing?
options: any man or woman who is qualified
items.explanation: The slash (technically a virgule) has few defensible uses beyond dates and lines of poetry. Garner: “Use it as a last resort.”

items.prompt: How does a dash change “The man from Ames, Iowa, arrived”?
options: “The man—he was from Ames, Iowa—arrived” — the dashes take over the commas' job
It doesn't; dashes and commas can be mixed freely
The commas must be kept inside the dashes
items.explanation: Dashes replace otherwise mandatory punctuation. That's why doubling up — comma plus dash — always looks wrong.

items.prompt: This app's house style — drawn from the judicial corpus — sets em dashes:
items.explanation: The Blue Book notes that some writers and publishers prefer spaces around dashes. Judge Grant and the current Supreme Court do not, so this app drills the closed form. Consistency is what matters.
